annotation.reasoning_summary: Polygons depict discrete housing-block/object footprints for housing association ownership, not a near-complete tessellation; the decisive entity rule is object-level housing assets with numeric attributes, not an amount layer.
Point layer of selected archaeological cesspits/find spots with addresses and photos; each point represents a discrete archaeological object/location, not a measurement or event.

Point features mark selected archaeological find locations; each point represents a discrete archaeological object/site entry with location, category, description, and object code, so this is an ObjectDS rather than an amount or event layer.

These polygons are selected archaeological site footprints, not a full-area partition; the map describes discrete archaeological finds/sites with names, addresses, and investigation details, so the decisive rules are plain region + object.
Polygons mark selected BBQ restriction/permission zones in parks, not a full-area partition; this fits patch zones rather than tessellation or objects.

Polygons are isolated conservation area boundaries, not a complete partition, so PlainVectorRegion. The layer represents named protected city/district conservation areas with status and designation dates, i.e. bounded real-world objects, so ObjectDS.
Point observations record wild bee inventories at locations and years; the decisive rule is event/occurrence at point locations rather than object or amount mapping.
Point locations show bee hives/colonies at each site, and the mapped main phenomenon is the numeric amount of colonies/hives (Aantal_volken / Aantal_kasten), so this is a point amount layer.

Polygon zones form a near-partition with strong tessellation hints. The layer is a full-area soil-quality classification with category fields for zone and soil function, so CoverageDS is the best fit.
Point map of individual trees with identifiers, species, height, owner and manager; the main phenomenon is discrete tree objects, not a measurement or event.
Point layer of individual trees; each feature is a distinct real-world object (tree) with descriptive attributes, so ObjectDS rather than AmountDS or EventDS.
Point layer of individual trees; each feature is a distinct real-world object, not a measurement or event.
Point features represent individual trees (distinct, countable objects) with species and planting attributes; numeric fields are object attributes, not the main phenomenon.
Point layer of discrete compost initiatives at street locations; each point represents a real-world facility/initiative, not a measurement or event.

Polygons are selected overlast/camera areas, not a full partition, so PlainVectorRegion. The layer represents bounded special zones of camera coverage around named places, which fits PatchDS rather than reporting units or full coverage.
Point features represent individual Canadian poplar trees with identifiers, species, and management status; this is an object layer, not a measurement or event layer.
Points represent discrete sensor/camera installations in the crowd monitoring system; this is an object layer, not a measurement or event layer.

Polygon areas mark selected culture-historical exploration zones and protected areas, not a full reporting tessellation; this fits bounded patch areas. The map is about culture-historical values of areas, so PatchDS is the best entity.
Point features represent individual knotweed sightings/locations; the numeric area field is just an attribute, so this is an object layer rather than amount or event.

Point features mark ecological barrier/passage locations, not measurements or objects. The layer is about selected issue sites and solution locations along the ecological network, so PatchDS fits better than ObjectDS or AmountDS.

Polygon features are isolated potential wind-energy sites rather than a tessellating area cover, so PlainVectorRegion. The decisive entity rule is object: each polygon is a distinct proposed wind-energy location with capacity/production attributes, not a coverage or amount map.

Point locations are voting stations, but the layer’s main phenomenon is the numeric election result at each station (votes, turnout, percentages). By the point-amount rule, this is AmountDS rather than ObjectDS.

Point features mark reported/remediated oak processionary caterpillar nest occurrences at tree locations, with real-time mutation dates; the decisive rule is event-at-point rather than object inventory.
Polygons mark selected pedicab prohibition/permission areas, not a full-area partition, so PlainVectorRegion; the theme is bounded restriction zones, so PatchDS.
Point layer of pedicab standplaatsen (pitches); each point is a distinct real-world location/object, not a measurement or event.
Point features represent individual BAG verblijfsobject/adres locations with a classified non-residential function; this is an object layer, not a measurement or event layer.

Polygon layer maps block-street function-mix classes (WON/VZN/WRK) with percentages, but polygons are not a complete tessellation of the study area; it is a selected thematic coverage of area units. CoverageDS fits the full-area categorical function classification, while topology hints support PlainVectorRegion.
Neighborhood administrative units form a near-complete polygon partition, so geometry is VectorTessellation. They are reporting/statistical areas with codes and attributes, so entity is LatticeDS.

Neighborhoods/buurten are reporting administrative units that partition the city area; topology strongly supports tessellation, and the layer is a lattice of statistical/administrative areas with codes and area attributes.
Neighborhood polygons form a near-complete administrative partition of Amsterdam, with strong tessellation topology and coded reporting-unit fields (Buurt, Buurtcombinatie_code, Stadsdeel_code).

Neighborhood polygons form a near-complete administrative partition with strong shared-boundary topology, so Geometry is VectorTessellation. The layer represents buurten/neighborhood reporting units with codes and area attributes, which fits LatticeDS.
City districts are administrative reporting units that partition Amsterdam, and the polygon topology strongly supports a tessellation.

These polygons are Amsterdam city districts, which are administrative/statistical reporting units forming a near-complete partition; classify as tessellation and LatticeDS despite numeric area attributes.

The layer represents Amsterdam area units (Buurten/Wijken/Gebieden/Stadsdelen) that partition the city, and the topology strongly supports a tessellation; the polygons are reporting/administrative units, so LatticeDS.

The polygons are Amsterdam gebieds/neighbourhood-style reporting units that form a near-complete partition, with strong tessellation topology hints. The decisive entity rule is reporting/statistical units -> LatticeDS.
This is a tessellated set of Amsterdam practice areas/stadsdelen that form an administrative/statistical partition. The decisive rule is reporting-unit geography, so Entity is LatticeDS.

Polygon regions form a near-partition of Amsterdam practice areas/neighbourhood units, with high shared boundaries and adjacency, so VectorTessellation. The named administrative/statistical areas with area attributes fit the reporting-unit rule, so LatticeDS.

Polygon noise-contour zones for industrial noise are selected bounded areas, not a full tessellation or reporting units; the decisive entity rule is patch (selected phenomenon zones), with polygons representing contour areas rather than objects or coverage.
Polygon contour zones for aircraft noise; the class bands (55-60, 60-65, etc.) indicate isoline/interval contours rather than reporting units or a full thematic coverage.

The layer shows noise-level polygon bands such as 50-55 dB and >70 dB, so the main phenomenon is contour/interval classification rather than reporting units. Although polygons are highly adjacent, the map is a set of noise contour zones, not a full administrative tessellation.

Polygon noise-contour bands with class labels like 50-55 dB and 55-60 dB indicate isoline/interval zones, so ContourDS. Despite many adjacent polygons, the polygons overlap and are contour fragments rather than a complete tessellation, so PlainVectorRegion.

Point features are voting locations/stembureaus, and the main mapped phenomenon is numeric vote totals and percentages shown by circle size; this is a point amount layer rather than point objects alone.
Point layer of identifiable green-roof locations/addresses in Amsterdam; the main phenomenon is discrete roof objects/projects, not measurements. Numeric fields are just attributes, so ObjectDS.
Land use polygons form a near-complete partition with strong tessellation topology; the coded classes indicate exhaustive area-wide thematic coverage rather than individual objects or patches.

The layer maps discrete historical buildings/sites as selectable places with names, functions, and dates. Geometry is points, and the main phenomenon is identifiable objects rather than events or amounts.

The layer depicts three selectable Amsterdam boundary shapes used as comparison objects, not a reporting-unit partition or full coverage. The decisive rule is object/area feature semantics with isolated polygons, so PlainVectorRegion + ObjectDS.

Polygon areas mark selected dog off-leash, prohibition, and restriction zones, not a full-area partition; topology also supports PlainVectorRegion. Entity is PatchDS because these are bounded special-use areas/phenomenon patches rather than objects or reporting units.

The layer maps selected green-structure areas and protected green zones, not a full-area partition or reporting units; polygons are discrete bounded patches. The decisive rule is PatchDS for selected phenomenon areas.
Point layer of individual elm trees; the decisive rule is ObjectDS for distinct real-world objects, with PointDS geometry.
Point features mark discrete housing projects/buildings with names, addresses, owners, and dwelling counts; the numeric field is an attribute, not the main phenomenon, so this is an object layer.

Point features represent individual chestnut trees, a set of identifiable objects. The numeric field is just an ID, and the layer is an object inventory with condition attributes, not a measurement layer.
Point features sample a continuous climate/hydrology field (Maaiveld, GLG, GLG_maaiveld), so this is a point measurement layer rather than objects or amounts.

The polygons form a near-partition with strong shared boundaries, so VectorTessellation. The layer maps flood risk classes by probability/depth bands, which are contour-like interval zones rather than objects or reporting units.
Point features represent named market locations with opening days/times; this is a set of discrete places/venues, not a measurement or event layer.
Point features representing discrete named green monuments/bomen with status and registry attributes; classify as object points, not amounts or events.
Point layer of individual monumental trees; each point represents a distinct real-world object, not a measurement or event.
Point features represent discrete monuments (buildings, artworks, sites) with status/type attributes; this is an object layer, not an amount or event layer.

Point layer of actual plant growth locations; the main mapped phenomenon is presence of protected quay wall flora, not numeric counts. The yearly Aantal fields are attributes, so existence/presence at points is the decisive rule.

The layer represents NO2 measurements at monitoring locations (stations/buisjes), so the main phenomenon is point-sampled environmental measurement. Geometry is point-based despite the MultiPolygon encoding, and the decisive entity rule is point measurements, not amount or object.
Point locations representing NO2 measurement sites; the main phenomenon is sampled air-quality measurements, not the points as objects. Rule used: point measurements at locations -> PointMeasuresDS.
Polygon layer for the Oergeul old-gulch area is a selected bounded zone, not a reporting unit or full-area coverage; topology also shows isolated polygons, supporting PlainVectorRegion and PatchDS.
Point layer of boreholes/soundings with depth measurements; main phenomenon is sampled ground/soil measurement data rather than objects or events.

Polygons represent named development neighbourhoods/projects rather than a full statistical partition, so PlainVectorRegion. The decisive entity rule is object-like bounded places/projects with codes and names, not amounts or coverage.
Point features representing discrete public toilet facilities and related access types; numeric price is just an attribute, so classify as ObjectDS rather than AmountDS.

The polygons are neighborhood-like areas with high shared boundaries, so they form a tessellation. The layer marks selected policy zones/conditions for overnight policy rather than a full reporting unit or object layer, so PatchDS fits best.

The polygons form a partition-like area-based zoning layer for parking standards, with strong tessellation hints and categorical area classes (A/B/C), so this is a VectorTessellation and a full-area thematic CoverageDS.

Polygons represent named parks and green spaces as discrete bounded objects, not a full tessellation; the park/plantsoen layer is object-focused, with area as an attribute rather than the main phenomenon.
Postcode4 areas are reporting/statistical units and the polygons form a near-complete partition with high shared boundaries, so this is a VectorTessellation and a LatticeDS.

Postcode4 areas are administrative/reporting units that partition the city closely, and the topology hints strongly support a tessellation. The decisive entity rule is reporting/statistical units -> LatticeDS, not AmountDS despite the area field.

The layer maps postcode6 polygon units with a postcode code attribute; these are reporting/statistical units rather than a full tessellation of the study area. Classified as LatticeDS, with PlainVectorRegion because the polygons are overlapping postcode areas and do not form a clean partition.
LineString infrastructure layer for plus and main transport networks; decisive rule is connected route/network system, not numeric attributes.

The layer maps pedestrian plus/hoofdnet infrastructure zones, i.e. a transport network system. Polygons are discrete network areas rather than a tessellated coverage, so PlainVectorRegion with NetworkDS.
Point layer of named camera/sensor locations; each point is a distinct real-world object, not a measurement or event. The decisive rule is object points.

Point layer of privacy-related camera/sensor locations; each point represents a monitored/privacy-processing occurrence tied to specific investigations and pilots, so PointDS with EventDS is the best fit.
Point layer of named scan/camera/sensor locations with addresses and privacy statements; each point represents a distinct real-world object, not a measurement or event.
Point features mark stemlocaties for the 2019 Provincial States election, and the main phenomenon is an election occurrence/result at each location, so PointDS + EventDS.

Polygons mark selected rainproof drainage concern areas with a categorical possible/not possible status, not a full-area tessellation or reporting units. This fits a bounded phenomenon patch rather than coverage or lattice.

Polygons are isolated hydro-unit areas tied to Rainproof problem locations and solution PDFs, not a full administrative/reporting tessellation. The layer represents bounded intervention/issue zones, so PatchDS; polygon topology also supports PlainVectorRegion.

These polygons are selected rainwater bottleneck zones/areas of concern, not a full tessellation or reporting units. The layer represents bounded problem patches identified by model analysis and expert review.
Polygon patches marking modeled rainproof sewerage problem locations; they are selected bounded zones, not a reporting-unit tessellation or full-area coverage.
Point features represent discrete religious buildings/places (churches, mosques, temples) with names, addresses, and categories, so this is PointDS with ObjectDS rather than amounts or events.
Line geometries representing sidewalk segments along streets; this is a connected transport/walking infrastructure network with width attributes, so NetworkDS.
LineString features describe roadway segments affected by the mopeds-on-roadway traffic decision, so this is a route/infrastructure network layer.
Point features represent discrete public sports/playground facilities (named locations with attributes like surface and fencing), so this is an object layer, not an amount or event layer.
Point locations of city farming sites; each point represents a distinct real-world place/facility with name, address, and status, so ObjectDS rather than AmountDS or EventDS.

Polygons represent named city farming sites/terrains (parks, school gardens, volkstuin complexes), not a reporting tessellation; topology also shows isolated polygons, supporting PlainVectorRegion. The main phenomenon is discrete bounded objects, so ObjectDS.
Point features mark where initiatives were established over the past years; the decisive rule is event/occurrence at locations, not point objects or amounts.
Major streets are a connected street infrastructure system, and the features are LineStrings; classify by the network rule.
Line geometry and the layer represents district heating/cooling transport infrastructure; the decisive rule is network/route system, with transport lines simplified for display.

Polygons are buffered representations of heat/cold network lines, not a full-area partition, so PlainVectorRegion. The main phenomenon is district heating/cooling infrastructure, a network system, despite polygon geometry.

Polygons are selected housing-planning project areas, not a complete tessellation; the layer mainly shows bounded development patches with project names and housing-capacity attributes, so PatchDS fits better than Lattice or Coverage.
Point features marking named local food/farming initiatives and farms with addresses and categories; this is a set of discrete real-world objects, not measurements or events.
Line geometries showing tram and metro lines/stations network; decisive rule is connected route/infrastructure system -> NetworkDS.
LineString features represent the tram and metro line network; metadata explicitly describes routes, stations, haltes, and lines, so this is a connected transport system (NetworkDS).
Point features represent tram stops/metro stations, but the layer is primarily a transit stop network with line membership attributes; network rule overrides object/amount.
Point features represent tram stops and metro stations, and the metadata says they are part of the tram/metro network; the numeric RADIUS is just an attribute, not the main phenomenon.
Point features represent distinct traffic-light-controlled intersections; the numeric fields are attributes/history, not the main phenomenon. Classified as object points.
Line network of Amsterdam roads with traffic prognosis values on each link; the main phenomenon is numeric traffic volume/projection on line features, so LineDS + AmountDS.

Point features are voting locations (stemlocaties). The layer mainly maps numeric election results at each point, with circle size representing vote counts/percentages, so this is PointDS with AmountDS.
Point features represent individual trees (identified by species, tree ID, planting year, size classes), so this is a point object layer rather than measurements or events.
Point features represent identifiable traffic information system objects (cameras, displays, poles) with names/IDs and attributes; this is an object layer, not an amount or event layer.
Point features represent distinct traffic information system installations (objects/assets) with IDs, type, and location metadata; not a measurement or event layer.
Point features mark discrete bird nesting locations at addresses; the main phenomenon is identifiable breeding sites/objects, not amounts or events.
Points represent discrete park benches, which are identifiable real-world objects; the numeric fields are just attributes, while the map mainly shows bench adoption status.

Line geometry representing street segments/sidewalk stretches; the main mapped phenomenon is walkability/available walking space and crowding ratings along the route network, so it fits a line-based amount/condition layer rather than objects or regions.
Point geometry with 226 features; each point marks a distinct wall-art artwork at a building address, so the main phenomenon is identifiable cultural objects, not measurements or events.

The polygons form a near-complete administrative-style partition of Amsterdam welstand areas, supported by high shared boundaries and adjacency; the layer is a full-area categorical classification of welstand levels, so CoverageDS.
Polygons form a near-complete area partition with strong tessellation hints, and the layer is a citywide thematic classification of welstand levels (full-area coverage by category), so CoverageDS.
Point layer of WWII attack/incidence locations with dates; main phenomenon is where and when events occurred, so PointDS + EventDS.

Polygons are discrete housing project areas, not a complete administrative tessellation, so PlainVectorRegion. The main mapped phenomenon is the housing plan quantities (Totaal and breakdown counts), making it an AmountDS rather than an object or patch layer.
Point layer of discrete self-build plot projects; each point represents a named plot/project with attributes, so ObjectDS rather than AmountDS or EventDS.

Polygon layer of individual buildings/daks with categorical suitability for solar panels on heritage sites; these are selected bounded zones rather than a reporting tessellation, so PatchDS with PlainVectorRegion.
Point features represent detected solar-panel installations, and the mapped meaning is the numeric amount/capacity (panel count and watt-peak). This fits point-based AmountDS rather than ObjectDS.
Points mark named swimming and play-water locations; they are discrete facilities/places, so this is an object layer rather than amount, event, or measurement.
